findings.antecedent: presence of shops (attractors)
findings.mechanism: Shops, as the basic attractors in urban areas, work, it seems, as logarithmic multipliers on a basic pattern of movement defined by configuration.
findings.quote: The effect of shops as attractors is to shift a basically linear relation between integration and movement into a logarithmic relation.

findings.antecedent: axial depth from the exterior in Maiden Lane estate
findings.mechanism: This rapid falloff in movement with depth is a very common property for housing estates, and shows graphically how spatial configuration freezes out all natural movement from the estate.

findings.antecedent: average integration of six equal-sized groups of spaces (integration bands)
findings.mechanism: divide the whole data set into a number of integration bands with equal numbers of spaces and check the average integration of these against mean movement rates.

findings.antecedent: integration values of eastern subarea lines (north of Gresham Street around Austin Friars) in City of London
findings.mechanism: shows narrow ranges both in natural movement rates and in integration, and clusters in a very small region of the scattergram, though retaining a reasonable correlation.

stimuli.description: Real urban environments in King's Cross area, City of London, South London housing estate, and Highgate study area.
Axial maps and black-on-white space maps representing urban grids.

tables.description: Mean encounter rates (in people per hundred metres per minute) for King's Cross area and subareas.
Mean spatial values, encounter rates, and correlation coefficients for ten subareas of King's Cross.
City of London-movement rates for each of the 5 time periods for the two central routes (route 1 and route 2).

limitations: It is not possible to ascertain how far the observed patterns are a result of grid properties and how it is a result of attractors, as it is not yet possible to excise areas from the larger system and compute their mean integration values read within the large system in order to compare them with mean encounter rates.
It is not possible to take the ten routes as representative of their well-defined areas.

Differences between local subareas in the City of London study may be the result of differential distribution of built forms or the distinctively regional character of the City grid, requiring further research.
Much remains to be understood about the ceteris paribus clause in the theory of natural movement.
